http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/19/seven.text: A tourist helicopter crashed at Kenya's Mount Ololokwe on Wednesday, killing all seven people on board, according to local authorities.The Kenyan Civil Aviation Authority said the incident occurred at around 9:13 am local time as the aircraft made its way from the Loisaba wildlife conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro river.The helicopter involved in the crash was a Eurocopter EC130 B4, it added.Video footage shared on social media appears to show the site of the crash, with black smoke visible against the foot of the mountain."There were 7 people on board the helicopter, one pilot and six passengers," Fredrick Kabunge, the director of the Aircraft Accident Investigation Department, told AFP, adding that the "helicopter was transporting tourists for a scenic flight" and confirming that there were no survivors.In a post on X, the Kenya Red Cross said its emergency response teams were at the scene of the crash in Samburu County and were working with other agencies to access the site."Search and recovery efforts are ongoing, hampered by difficult terrain access and an active fire at the crash site," it said in an update later on Wednesday. "An additional team has been dispatched from Isiolo to reinforce the operation."This is a developing story. Check back later for further details.

As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in Simon Tisdall The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands Sun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 06.15 EDT Share U kraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs , pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost. Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan . Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties , his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff , back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity. This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it? The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022, then left them to sink or swim . Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors and paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’s nauseating Alaska summit , and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price. Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About 60% oppose ceding Donbas land to Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians also want it to stop . And like Moscow, Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch , notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly a deal to be done . But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away. View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump meet at the Elmendorf-Richardson military facility in Alaska, 15 August 2026. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Efforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has now extended to the Red Sea (Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modern forever war phenomenon . Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but to win a Nobel peace prize (plus lucrative Russian energy deals). Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas. Trump’s “board of peace” and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fear fighting will drag on indefinitely . Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together. Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led to war crime atrocities such as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedly killed more than 100 schoolgirls in February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy. Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightly restricted international journalists’ access to Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost of successful Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict. Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Western democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly, urged here ) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war. https://www.miragenews.com/film-brings-u.text: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News World 05 Oct 2026 3:20 am AEDT Date Time Share The United Nations A documentary drawn from United Nations University research was screened at the COP30 climate conference and film festivals across Europe. Its most important journey, though, was the one back to the Mexico City canals where it was filmed. Scientific reports rarely leave the shelf. Sometimes, though, the research itself becomes a real story that sparks conversations far beyond academia. That is what happened in Xochimilco, in Mexico City. In 2025, the UN University Institute for Environment and Human Security ( UNU-EHS ) published a report on interconnected risks. It asked why societies struggle to make the changes needed to tackle climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. One conclusion: societies must think beyond the short term and weigh the wellbeing of future generations. To bring that idea to life, the researchers turned to Xochimilco. For centuries, its chinamperos have cultivated chinampas - fertile plots built on wetlands that produce food while preserving knowledge handed down through generations. Today that living heritage faces urbanization, environmental degradation, climate change and a shifting relationship between young people and the land. The result was a documentary, Chinamperos: Preserving Ancestral Farming Practices in Mexico City, directed by Mexican filmmaker Rodrigo Jardón Galeana and shot in San Gregorio Atlapulco. The aim was simple - take a scientific report off the page and show what it means for people at the centre of it in real terms. A call that reverberated Mariana Páez, one of those featured, shared the film on social media expecting family, friends and neighbours to watch. Instead, she also heard from people she had not spoken to in years. Among them were Karen Ramírez and Abel Bastida, former schoolmates on different career paths who shared a fascination with the place where they grew up. A video call planned for 20 or 30 minutes ran to nearly two hours - farming, food, traditions, water, the problems they saw around them. "We couldn't stop talking," Ms. Páez recalls. That conversation led the three to found the Permanent Seminar on Xochimilco Studies, or SEPEX, to open up dialogue about the territory and its culture. A film meant to communicate research had sparked a local conversation nobody had seen coming. Heard at last The documentary has since been screened at COP30 in Brazil and at festivals in Spain, Greece, Türkiye and the Czech Republic. Our colleagues in the UN News Spanish team also told the chinamperos' story in April 2025 . For Ms. Páez, though, the most important effects were closer to home. In her own family, the film brought greater recognition to work and Indigenous knowledge that had not always been valued like other professions. One of those featured, chinampero Samuel Avelino, died earlier this year. Ms. Páez later discovered that a screenshot of the UN News story carrying his testimony was among the last things he shared on Facebook. "He felt heard," she says. That matters, she explains, because the everyday lives of chinamperos rarely reach beyond their own circles. Outsiders rarely ask what a day working the land is like. Coming home More than a year on, the film returned to Mexico. SEPEX helped organize a visit to Xochimilco for representatives of the University and the UN in Mexico, and screenings followed at the National Centre for the Arts and the Metropolitan Autonomous University. Residents, researchers, students, UN staff and city officials came together. The aim was not just to show a film, but to let the community speak directly to researchers and decision makers. "Xochimilco is a living territory," said Allegra Baiocchi, the UN Resident Coordinator in Mexico - a place where biodiversity, water management, climate adaptation, food security and ancestral knowledge all converge. For Shen Xiaomeng , Vice-Rector of the University in Europe and Director of UNU-EHS, the trip was a chance to give something back. Meeting chinampero Eric Enríquez, she noted the pride with which he spoke about his work. Farmers' survival, she said, depends on how much society values them - but everyone else depends on those who grow our food. A window, not a solution Ms. Ramírez sees the film not as a solution but as a "window". It's a way of looking at what may lie ahead before deciding what to do. She wants it screened in more neighbourhoods and public spaces across Xochimilco, with children joining the conversations. Mr. Bastida stresses that Xochimilco is not simply a landscape in need of preservation. People live there, with different needs and different visions of its future. The documentary does not resolve those differences. But it has done something less visible, and perhaps necessary before any solution can emerge: created a place where people can meet on common ground and talk about them. /UN News Release.
